title: TLS loss in superconducting resonators on epitaxial hBN thin films
authors: J. Christiansen-Salameh, D. J. Temples, R. Linehan, S. Sussman, Aloyse Maille, F. Abouzahr, L. Alexis, K. Anyang, D. Bowring, G. Bratrud, E. Celi, A. H. Colón Cesaní, R. Khatiwada, D. Molenaar, O. Peek, A. Rodriguez, O. Seidel, D. Schlom, D. Sotir, S. Uemura, Y. Wu, E. Figueroa-Feliciano, D. Baxter, Z. Tian
abstract: The integration of low-loss dielectrics into superconducting circuits is of importance to the functionality of quantum computers and sensors. In this work, we fabricate and measure niobium resonators atop few-layer, epitaxial hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy on a sapphire substrate and compare against a control counterpart without hBN. We conduct radiofrequency measurements which probe the responses to power, temperature, and temporal fluctuations of two-level systems. The resonators integrating hBN maintain low dielectric loss with a low-power internal loss tangent on the order of $10^{-6}$, and demonstrate hBN can be added to the conventional superconducting qubit stack with minimal degradation of the quality factor. This research represents a first step towards a materials-driven strategy to eliminate phonon-mediated correlated errors in solid-state quantum systems, which leverages the thermal properties of 2D materials to prevent athermal phonons excited in the device substrate from transmitting across the superconductor-substrate interface. The same technique applied to quantum sensors would maximize phonon collection by blocking phonons from entering passive metal films.
summary: This experimental work investigates using epitaxial hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) as a low-loss dielectric interface layer for superconducting resonators. By measuring resonator quality factors under varying power and temperature, the authors demonstrate that hBN significantly helps maintain low dielectric loss, offering a materials-driven pathway to reduce decoherence in solid-state quantum computing platforms.
main_problem: The primary goal is to mitigate energy loss and decoherence in superconducting circuits, specifically addressing losses caused by phonon-mediated quasiparticle bursts and Two-Level Systems (TLS).
main_result: The integration of epitaxial hBN thin films into superconducting resonators maintains low dielectric loss, suggesting hBN can be used to suppress phonon-mediated errors in quantum devices.
method: The researchers fabricated niobium resonators on epitaxial hBN films and performed radiofrequency measurements, including power and temperature sweeps, to characterize various loss mechanisms.
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting resonator (Nb film) fabricated atop few-layer, epitaxial hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) grown on sapphire. The mechanism studied involves the interaction between the superconductor and the substrate interface, where hBN is hypothesized to reflect detrimental athermal phonons.
key_observables: Resonator Quality Factor (Q), dielectric loss tangent ($	an \delta$), internal loss ($\delta_i$), and the power/temperature dependence of TLS loss components.
important_parameters: Low-power internal loss tangent on the order of $10^{-6}$; superconducting gap energy ($2\Delta$); temperature range (15–300 mK); and the presence of the hBN interface.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that the epitaxial hBN film effectively reflects and diffuses athermal phonons, thereby protecting the superconducting circuit from substrate-induced energy loss.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the concept of phonon reflection by 2D materials, show resonance fits extracting Q factors, and present power and temperature dependence plots for various loss components.
paper_structure: The paper details the MBE growth of hBN, the sputtering/etching process for the Nb resonators, and then proceeds to cryogenic measurements analyzing the power and temperature dependence of the resonator's loss characteristics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses material science challenges in superconducting quantum hardware by proposing a 2D material interface engineering solution to reduce decoherence sources, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems.
